# Deuteronomy 32:27–52 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

## v. 27 — *if I had not dreaded the taunt of the enemy, lest their adversaries misunderstand and say: "Our own hand has prevailed; it was not the LORD who did all this."*

**Traditional reading:** God refrained from utterly destroying Israel — not because they deserved mercy, but for His own Name's sake. The language of "dreading" or "fearing" is anthropomorphic (God speaking after the manner of men). Moses had pleaded this very argument in Numbers 14:13–16 and Exodus 32:12, but here it is God Himself who says it. The point is that if God completely wiped out Israel, the pagan nations would boast that their own military might — not Yahweh's judgment — had brought Israel down.

- Ellicott: "The argument of these verses is such as no man would dare to put into the mouth of the Most High. Moses had pleaded it … but none but Jehovah Himself would say for Himself, 'I feared the wrath of the enemy.'" "Behave themselves strangely" may mean "misunderstand it" or "take note of it (as a strange thing)." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Three interpretations are offered — (1) God feared being provoked by the enemy's boasting; (2) God feared wrath coming upon the enemy; (3) God feared the enemy would be emboldened against Israel. The first is most approved. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Gill: God speaks after the manner of men; this denotes His "precaution, provision, and preparation … to put a check upon it … that he might not have the opportunity of instilling it into the minds of men, that God was cruel to his people, or had not ability to save them." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Enduring Word (Guzik): "One thing that would soften the judgment of Yahweh against Israel would be the pride and arrogance of the other nations God would use to punish Israel. … One reason God would spare and restore Israel was because the pride of their adversaries." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

**No major tradition-specific differences identified in the sources consulted for this verse.**

---

## v. 28 — *Israel is a nation devoid of counsel, with no understanding among them.*

**Traditional reading:** This verse describes either Israel or the enemy nations (interpreters differ). If it refers to Israel, it laments their foolishness in failing to understand that their defeat came from God's hand. If it refers to the enemy nations (as Wesley held), it laments that they are too foolish to recognize Yahweh's role.

- Wesley: "Their enemies are foolish people, and therefore make so false and foolish a judgment upon things." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Ellicott: "Void of counsel.—Literally, perishing in counsels, or, perhaps, spoiling the plans of Jehovah." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Pulpit: Israel was "a people utterly destitute of counsel and without understanding." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/32.htm
- StudyLight (Speaker's Commentary): "For the reason they deserved not to be spared." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/32-27.html

---

## v. 29 — *If only they were wise, they would understand it; they would comprehend their fate.*

**Traditional reading:** A lament over Israel's lack of wisdom. If they had wisdom, they would "consider their latter end" — that is, look ahead to where their present path of rebellion was leading: destruction.

- Pulpit: "If they were wise they would understand this. They would consider their latter end! i.e. the end to which they were going, the inevitable issue of the course they were taking." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Ellicott: "Have some discernment as to their hereafter, what their destiny was, and what they will miss, if they fail to fulfil it." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Enduring Word (Guzik): "God wanted Israel to think about where their backsliding would lead them, what the end of their path would be." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

---

## v. 30 — *How could one man pursue a thousand, or two put ten thousand to flight, unless their Rock had sold them, unless the LORD had given them up?*

**Traditional reading:** This reverses the covenant blessing of Leviticus 26:8 (where obedient Israel would have one chase a thousand). When Israel is defeated in such lopsided fashion, the only explanation is that Yahweh — their Rock — has "sold" them and "given them up" into enemy hands. The rhetorical question expects the answer: "It could never happen unless God Himself abandoned them."

- Ellicott: "Comp. the verse in Deuteronomy 28:25, and more especially Leviticus 26:8; 26:17; 26:36." "Had sold them.—Here first used of Jehovah. It is a common expression in the book of Judges." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Pulpit: "If Israel were wise, they could easily overcome all their foes through the help of the Almighty (Leviticus 26:8); but having forsaken him, they were left by him, and so came under the power of the enemy." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Enduring Word (Guzik): "This was the opposite of the blessing God promised to an obedient Israel … When Israel was unfaithful to their covenant with Yahweh, He would give them to their enemies." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

---

## v. 31 — *For their rock is not like our Rock, even our enemies concede.*

**Traditional reading:** Even the pagan enemies themselves, if they were honest judges, would have to admit that their idol-gods ("their rock") are nothing compared to Yahweh ("our Rock"). Some take "their rock" here as referring to Israel's false rock (their idols), and "our Rock" as Yahweh. Others see "their rock" as the enemies' gods.

- Pulpit: "The heathen had also a rock in which they trusted — their idol-gods; but even the heathen themselves being judges, their rock was not to be compared with the true God." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Ellicott: "For their rock (the enemies' God) is not as our Rock (Jehovah), and yet our enemies are judges, i.e., lords, over us. … No cause can be found for the defeat of Israel except the displeasure of Jehovah." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Enduring Word (Guzik): notes this as part of the description of Israel's wickedness under the vine/grapes imagery. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

---

## vv. 32–33 — *But their vine is from the vine of Sodom … Their grapes are poisonous; their clusters are bitter. Their wine is the venom of serpents, the deadly poison of cobras.*

**Traditional reading:** Most traditional commentators understand "their vine" as referring to Israel's spiritual corruption — her character had become like Sodom and Gomorrah. Others (like Kalland, cited in Guzik) apply these verses to Israel's enemies. The imagery of poisonous grapes and serpent-venom wine vividly pictures how Israel's fruit had become deadly rather than life-giving.

- Ellicott: "Their vine—i.e., Israel's … Comp. Hosea 10:1: 'Israel is an empty vine' … and Isaiah 5:2, 7: 'He looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes.'" — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Pulpit: Describes Israel's corrupt vine in contrast to the true Vine. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Enduring Word (Guzik), citing Kalland: "Under the figure of vines, grapes, and wine, the wickedness of Israel's enemies is described. Their vine (character) has its source in the vine of Sodom and Gomorrah … The grapes from their vine were filled with poison, bitterness, and snake venom." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/ (Kalland applies this to Israel's enemies; Ellicott and Pulpit apply it to Israel.)

**Tradition difference:** There is a divergence among commentators on whether "their vine" refers to Israel (Ellicott, Pulpit) or Israel's enemies (Kalland). This affects whether the passage is describing Israel's corruption or the wickedness of the pagan nations. Guzik's Enduring Word notes both possibilities but leans toward the enemy interpretation via Kalland.

---

## v. 34 — *"Have I not stored up these things, sealed up within My vaults?"*

**Traditional reading:** God keeps a record of the sins and the judgments due. "These things" refers either to the sins of Israel's enemies that call for vengeance, or to the calamities God has in store. The imagery of a sealed vault or treasury indicates that God's future judgments are certain, stored up, and ready.

- Ellicott: "'This' is generally taken to refer to what follows, but it is not clear. It may refer to the fact that 'He looked for grapes, and the vine brought forth wild grapes.'" — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Utley (NASB): "'Is it not laid up in store with Me, Sealed up in My treasuries?'" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-32.html
- Enduring Word (Guzik): the verse serves as a transition to the pronouncement of divine vengeance in verse 35. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

---

## v. 35 — *Vengeance is Mine; I will repay. In due time their foot will slip; for their day of disaster is near, and their doom is coming quickly.*

**Traditional reading:** This is one of the most quoted verses in the New Testament (Romans 12:19; Hebrews 10:30). God reserves vengeance to Himself; human beings are not to take it into their own hands. The imagery of a slipping foot suggests sudden, unexpected judgment. Jonathan Edwards built his famous sermon *"Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God"* on this very phrase, "their foot shall slip in due time."

- Thompson (cited in Guzik): "Verse 35 is quoted in the New Testament in Romans 12:19 and Hebrews 10:30. … No individual should assume that he can carry out the divine sentence by the exercise of his own vengeful feelings." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Edwards (summarized by Guzik) developed these points from this verse: (1) Sinners are always in danger of judgment; they stand in a slippery place. (2) Sinners are in danger of sudden judgment. (3) Sinners are to be blamed for their own fall. (4) Sinners' fall is delayed only by God's mercy; judgment will come "in due time." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Ellicott: Notes the quotation in Hebrews 10:30 with Deuteronomy 32:36a. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm

**Tradition note:** The NT use in Romans 12:19 is universal across traditions — it grounds the Christian ethic of non-retaliation. The verse is also foundational for the doctrine of divine justice across Reformed, Baptist, Methodist, and other traditions.

---

## v. 36 — *For the LORD will vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants when He sees that their strength is gone and no one remains, slave or free.*

**Traditional reading:** God's judgment on Israel is not final — it is disciplinary and purifying. When Israel is brought to the end of their own strength, utterly helpless, then God will "vindicate" (or "judge") His people and show compassion. The phrase "judge His people" can be understood as "vindicate" or "defend" His people (as in Psalm 135:14, where this verse is quoted verbatim). It is when human power is completely exhausted that divine deliverance comes.

- Enduring Word (Guzik): "God's judgment of His people is an expression of His compassion. He judges them to discipline them, to train them, to purify them." Also notes the alternate sense of "vindicate." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Kalland (cited in Guzik): "The Lord's vindication comes when his people have no more strength and, hyperbolically, no longer exist." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Ellicott: "'Shall judge' means 'shall punish,' not 'shall defend' " — but notes it is quoted together with verse 35 in Hebrews 10:30. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Utley: "For the Lord will vindicate His people, And will have compassion on His servants, When He sees that their strength is gone." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-32.html

**Tradition difference:** Ellicott takes "judge" as punish; Guzik/Kalland take it as "vindicate." The ambiguity reflects a genuine tension in the Hebrew, and both senses are theologically true.

---

## vv. 37–38 — *He will say: "Where are their gods, the rock in which they took refuge, which ate the fat of their sacrifices … Let them rise up and help you; let them give you shelter!"*

**Traditional reading:** God taunts the helpless idols. In Israel's hour of crisis, the false gods they trusted — which "ate" the fat of their sacrifices — would be powerless to help. The language is bitingly ironic. Ellicott notes that God did say this very thing in Judges 10:14.

- Ellicott: "He did say so in Judges 10:14." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Enduring Word (Guzik): "God would put the severe judgments … to a good purpose: to destroy Israel's confidence in the gods of the nations. They would be of no help to Israel." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Utley: "And He will say, 'Where are their gods, The rock in which they sought refuge? Who ate the fat of their sacrifices … Let them rise up and help you.'" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-32.html

---

## v. 39 — *See now that I am He; there is no God besides Me. I bring death and I give life; I wound and I heal, and there is no one who can deliver from My hand.*

**Traditional reading:** This is one of the great monotheistic declarations of the OT. The emphatic doubled "I" (I, even I, am He) stresses God's unique self-existence. He alone holds absolute sovereignty over life, death, wounding, and healing. The verse is understood both temporally (God controls physical life and death) and spiritually/covenantally (He kills and revives the nation). Christians see this as a Christological text: Jesus quotes the language "I am He" (ἐγώ εἰμι, John 8:24; 18:5), and Revelation 1:8 echoes it.

- Gill: "Christ is the sovereign disposer of life and death, of sickness and health … in a spiritual sense he wounds and kills, by the law in the hand of his Spirit; and he heals and makes alive by his Gospel." Also notes the Targum of Jerusalem: "I am he that kills the living in this world, and quickens the dead in the world to come." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Ellicott: "I kill, and I make alive.—This was repeated by Hannah in her song (1 Samuel 2:6). Comp. also Isaiah 43:13." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Matthew Henry: "Though he kill, yet he makes alive again: though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/deuteronomy-32.html
- Keil (cited on BibleHub): "These words do not refer to the immortality of the soul, but to the restoration of life of the people of Israel, which God had delivered up to death." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/32-39.htm

**Tradition differences:** 
- **Reformed/Calvinistic** reading emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty: He decrees both death and life, wounding and healing — all under His control, including reprobation and election.
- **Wesleyan/Arminian** reading (Wesley): "Learn by your own sad experience what vain and impotent things idols are." The emphasis is on the experiential lesson and human responsibility. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/deuteronomy/32.htm
- **Charismatic/Pentecostal** traditions (Guzik/Enduring Word represents broadly charismatic evangelicalism) often emphasize that God both wounds and heals today — linking this to divine healing.

---

## vv. 40–42 — *For I lift up My hand to heaven and declare: As surely as I live forever, when I sharpen My flashing sword … I will take vengeance on My adversaries … I will make My arrows drunk with blood …*

**Traditional reading:** This is God swearing an oath ("As I live forever") — the lifting of the hand to heaven is the ancient gesture of oath-taking (cf. Revelation 10:5–6). God presents Himself as a Divine Warrior arming for battle. The graphic imagery of arrows drunk with blood and a sword devouring flesh is poetic language for the totality of divine judgment.

- Thompson (cited in Guzik): "The expression my glittering sword means literally 'the lightning of my sword' … Yahweh is pictured as a warrior arming himself for battle (Exodus 15:3; Isaiah 42:13; 59:17)." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Ellicott: "For I lift up my hand.—This is the form in taking an oath. (Comp. Revelation 10:5.)" — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Enduring Word (Guzik): Notes that Jesus' teaching on oaths (Matthew 5:33–37) does not mean oaths are never appropriate — God Himself takes an oath here. The point is that daily speech should be so truthful that oaths are unnecessary. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

---

## v. 43 — *Rejoice, O heavens, with Him, and let all God's angels worship Him. Rejoice, O nations, with His people; for He will avenge the blood of His children … He will cleanse His land and His people.*

**Traditional reading:** The Song ends on a note of universal praise. Heaven, angels, and all nations are summoned to rejoice. The verse is quoted in the NT at two key points: Hebrews 1:6 ("let all God's angels worship Him") applies it to Christ, and Romans 15:10 ("Rejoice, O nations, with His people") applies it to the inclusion of Gentiles in God's saving purposes.

- Ellicott: "This is cited by St. Paul to show that the Gentiles must also 'glorify God for His mercy' in sending Jesus Christ. But it is not wholly fulfilled yet. 'If the fall of God's people was the wealth of the world … what will the receiving of them be, but life from the dead?' (Romans 11:12, 15; 15:10)." Also notes that the LXX has a longer version: "Rejoice, ye heavens, with Him, and let all the angels of God worship Him (Hebrews 1:7 [sic]); Rejoice, ye Gentiles, with His people." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Enduring Word (Guzik): "The Gentiles could come to understand what Israel came to know through the judgments of God against them … This atonement would be ultimately provided in Jesus Christ, who is the Savior not only of Israel, but of the whole world." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Wesley: "He calls upon the nations to rejoice and bless God … especially for the last wonderful deliverance which shall be given to the Jews, when they shall be converted to the gospel in the last days." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/deuteronomy/32.htm

**Textual/Septuagint note:** The BSB translation ("Rejoice, O heavens, with Him, and let all God's angels worship Him") follows the LXX reading, which is quoted in Hebrews 1:6. The Masoretic Hebrew Text is shorter and reads differently. The Dead Sea Scrolls support a longer Hebrew text closer to the LXX. This is a significant textual variation.

---

## vv. 44–45 — *Then Moses came with Joshua son of Nun and recited all the words of this song in the hearing of the people. When Moses had finished reciting all these words to all Israel …*

**Traditional reading:** Moses, accompanied by Joshua (called Hoshea here by some traditions), delivered the song publicly to the whole assembly. The partnership of Moses and Joshua in this act underscores Joshua's role as successor and ensures the song would be remembered.

- Wesley: "Probably Moses spoke it to as many as could hear him, while Joshua in another assembly at the same time delivered it to as many as his voice would reach. Thus Joshua, as well as Moses, would be a witness against them." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Enduring Word (Guzik): "The Song of Moses was presented to all Israel so they could learn from it and be warned by it." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Utley: notes the historical transition: Moses and Joshua together. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-32.html

---

## v. 46 — *he said to them, "Take to heart all these words I testify among you today, so that you may command your children to carefully follow all the words of this law."*

**Traditional reading:** Moses calls for heartfelt internalization, not mere external hearing. The command to teach children underscores the generational transmission of covenant faithfulness. "Take to heart" (literally "set your hearts") is a Qal imperative — an urgent command for deliberate, conscious commitment.

- Utley: "This VERB … is a Qal IMPERATIVE. Israel has a choice, an informed choice based on YHWH's past actions and current promises." Also: " 'you shall command your sons' — This emphasizes the educational responsibility of parents." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-32.html
- Enduring Word (Guzik): "As Israel received and responded to the word of God through Moses, their departure from Yahweh and His judgment following it would be delayed. If they and their children would observe God's law, they would be blessed and not cursed." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

---

## v. 47 — *For they are not idle words to you, because they are your life, and by them you will live long in the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess.*

**Traditional reading:** God's word is not empty or futile — it is life itself. This verse is a powerful statement about the vitality and efficacy of the word of God. Obedience brings prolonged days in the land. Theologically, it connects to Deuteronomy 8:3 ("man does not live by bread alone but by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD") and to the concept of God's word having independent power once spoken (Isaiah 55:11).

- Utley: "This is the concept of God's word as having an independent power once spoken (cf. Deut. 8:3; Psalms 33:6, 9; Isaiah 55:11). This word (Moses' writings) can bring life and health or death and destruction. Obedience is the continuing key to its effectiveness!" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-32.html
- Enduring Word (Guzik): "One of Satan's great lies is that it is a futile thing to serve God and obey His word. It sometimes seems that those who are against God prosper more … but it is not a futile thing to serve God." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Matthew Henry: "It is not a vain thing, because it is your life. It is not an indifferent thing, but of absolute necessity; it is not a trifle, but a matter of consequence, a matter of life and death." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/deuteronomy-32.html (via 32:44)

---

## v. 48 — *On that same day the LORD said to Moses …*

**Traditional reading:** The timing is significant — "on that same day" ties this divine command directly to the delivery of the Song. As soon as Moses had finished his prophetic work, God spoke about his death. Moses had completed his final task.

- Wesley: "Now he had finished his work, why should he desire to live a day longer? He had indeed formerly desired and prayed, that he might go over Jordan: but now he is entirely satisfied, and saith no more of that matter." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Constable: "The same day Moses gave his song to the Israelites God directed him to prepare for his death." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-32.html

---

## v. 49 — *"Go up into the Abarim Range to Mount Nebo, in the land of Moab across from Jericho, and view the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites as their own possession."*

**Traditional reading:** Mount Nebo is the highest peak in the Abarim mountain range, located east of the Jordan across from Jericho. From its summit one can see a panoramic view of the Promised Land. The command sequence uses multiple imperatives: "go up," "look at." God's gift of seeing the land, even without entering it, was an act of grace.

- Utley: "The last acts of Moses are scripted by a God who loved him, used him, and held him responsible for his actions!" Notes the imperatives: go up, look at, die, be gathered. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-32.html
- Constable: "People in that culture associated heights with nearness to deity, so perhaps both Aaron and Moses died and were buried on mountains to symbolize their nearness to God." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-32.html
- Enduring Word (Guzik): "The modern Mount Nebo provides a fine view over the Jordan valley and is traditionally identified with the site." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

---

## v. 50 — *And there on the mountain that you climb, you will die and be gathered to your people, just as your brother Aaron died on Mount Hor and was gathered to his people.*

**Traditional reading:** "Gathered to your people" is a Hebrew idiom for death that implies continued existence beyond the grave — reunion with ancestors. Aaron's death on Mount Hor (Numbers 20:22–29; 33:38–39) serves as the precedent, making Moses' own death less frightening. Matthew Henry notes that thinking of loved ones who have gone before is a great comfort in death.

- Matthew Henry: "It is a great encouragement to us, when we die, to think of our friends that have gone before us through that darksome valley, especially of Christ, our elder brother and great high priest." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/deuteronomy-32.html
- Utley: "The implication of the verse is that this will be the end of Moses' earthly life, but he will live on with his family and countrymen who have died before." Also notes the textual question: Deuteronomy 10:6 says Aaron died at Moserah, but "Hard Sayings of the Bible … says Moserah is the name of the area and Mount Hor the name of the specific mountain." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-32.html
- Constable: notes that Moses' sin at Kadesh prevented him from entering. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-32.html

---

## v. 51 — *For at the waters of Meribah-kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin, both of you broke faith with Me among the Israelites by failing to treat Me as holy in their presence.*

**Traditional reading:** This recalls the incident in Numbers 20:1–13 where Moses struck the rock instead of speaking to it as God commanded. God publicly names the sin: Moses "broke faith" and failed to "treat Me as holy" (sanctify God). The sin was not merely striking instead of speaking — it was misrepresenting God's character before the people. Moses' public leadership role meant his sin had public consequences.

- Constable (citing Merrill): "The Lord had told him to speak to the rock (Numbers 20:8), the mere act of speaking being designed to demonstrate the power of God who creates by the spoken word. To strike the rock was to introduce an interruptive element and thus to diminish the significance of the powerful word. By doing this, Moses betrayed not only anger and disobedience but he correspondingly reflected on the God whom he served." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-32.html
- Utley: "Moses' open and obvious disobedience before all the people … caused him to be publicly judged by God and not allowed to enter the Promised Land." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-32.html
- Wesley: "God reminds him of the sin he had committed long before. It is good for the holiest of men to die repenting, even of their early sins." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/deuteronomy/32.htm

---

## v. 52 — *Although you shall see from a distance the land that I am giving the Israelites, you shall not enter it.*

**Traditional reading:** This is both judgment and mercy. The judgment: Moses may not enter the Promised Land. The mercy: he is permitted to see it, which is more than the rebellious generation received. The sight from Mount Nebo became a symbol of faith — seeing the promises from afar without fully possessing them in this life (cf. Hebrews 11:13).

- Wesley: "Yet thou shalt see the land — And see it as the earnest of that better country, which is only seen with the eye of faith. What is death to him who has a believing prospect and a steadfast hope of eternal life?" — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/deuteronomy/32.htm
- Matthew Henry: "The remembrance of his sin might make death terrible, but the sight God gave him of Canaan took off the terror of it, as it was a token of God's being reconciled to him." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/deuteronomy-32.html
- Constable: "God permitted Moses to see the whole land of Canaan even though his sin at Kadesh prevented him from entering it." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-32.html
- Enduring Word (Guzik): "Moses, as the last act of his 120 years, would climb Mount Nebo, and die at the summit of the mountain." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Differences Identified

1. **Reformed tradition** (seen through Ligonier/Spurgeon-influenced sources): Emphasis on God's absolute sovereignty in verses 39–42 — God alone decrees who lives and dies, wounds and heals. The "vengeance is Mine" (v. 35) undergirds the Reformed understanding that human beings must not take vengeance into their own hands; this is quoted in Romans 12:19, a key text for Reformed ethics.

2. **Wesleyan/Methodist** (Wesley's Notes): More emphasis on the experiential and moral lesson — "learn by your own sad experience." Wesley reads v. 43 as pointing toward a future conversion of the Jews. He also stresses the importance of dying in a state of repentance (v. 51).

3. **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word / Guzik): Emphasis on the supernatural dimension — the demons behind idols (vv. 15–18 context), the power of God's word as life (v. 47), and the application of "I wound and I heal" (v. 39) to divine healing today.

4. **Baptist** (Gill's Exposition, from a Particular Baptist perspective): Strong Christological reading throughout — e.g., "the Rock" in v. 31 as Christ, with extended application of "I kill and I make alive" to Christ's work through the law and gospel. Gill sees Christ in nearly every verse.

5. **Text-critical scholarship** (Ellicott, Constable, Utley): Notably, v. 43 in the LXX contains an additional line about angels worshipping God, quoted in Hebrews 1:6. The Dead Sea Scrolls (4QDeutᵠ) support a longer Hebrew text. This is a well-known textual variant where the NT follows the Septuagintal tradition.
